The Treasury Department will automatically enroll more than 60 million additional children in Trump Accounts, potentially bringing the program to about 70 million accounts.

Trump Accounts Auto-Enrollment

On Tuesday, the Treasury Department released new rules that eliminate the need for parents to initially sign up their children for Trump Accounts, expanding access to the investment program.

Treasury said more than 60 million additional children under 18 will be automatically enrolled. About 7 million children have signed up so far, out of roughly 73 million eligible children.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this month that the number of accounts could reach about "70 million because we will go to auto-enroll," reported The Hill.

Trump Accounts Launch

President Donald Trump highlighted the launch of Trump Accounts in July. The tax-deferred investment accounts were created for eligible U.S. children under 18, with those born between 2025 and 2028 eligible for a one-time $1,000 Treasury contribution.

Parents, guardians, and other authorized individuals could open one account per child, with contributions invested in a fund that tracks the S&P 500.

Beginning July 4, 2026, families and others could contribute up to $5,000 annually per child, while employers could contribute up to $2,500.

Trump Accounts Expansion

Earlier this month, Trump Accounts received backing from billionaires including Michael Dell and Ray Dalio, with Dell pledging $6.25 billion and Dalio offering to match $250 donations for eligible Connecticut children.

Bessent also launched a "50 State Challenge" to encourage more philanthropic support, while Elon Musk said he would not contribute.

Last month, Robinhood Markets Inc. (NASDAQ:HOOD) CEO Vlad Tenev said the accounts gave children access to the S&P 500 through a low-cost State Street ETF, to introduce investing from birth.

In July, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano said the government aimed to enroll all 70 million children under 18, with officials working with tax-preparation companies and banks to simplify enrollment. At the time, about 6.5 million children had enrolled.

Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA) delivered sharp criticism of President Donald Trump on Tuesday, reaffirming that the latter favors oil companies over consumers as the administration rolled back fuel economy standards.

Massive Wealth Transfer to Oil Companies

In a post on X, Newsom quoted a post by Reuters that said the rolling back of the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards will increase gas consumption and emissions.

The White House did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for a comment.

“After forcing us to pay $120 BILLION more for fuel because of his idiotic war with Iran,” Newsom said, “Donald Trump is now rolling back fuel standards so new cars get even fewer miles per gallon,” he added. Newsom called the move a “massive wealth transfer” from ordinary Americans to oil companies.

Newsom had earlier criticized the move, saying that the rollback would increase emissions and pollution, while also pointing to record-high gas prices at the pump since the war with Iran kicked off in February this year.

According to data from the American Automobile Association (AAA), the national average price of gas was down to $4.4558/gallon on Tuesday. However, California’s average price of gas jumped to $6.3803/gallon on Tuesday.

Sean Duffy Backs CAFE Rollback

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy backed Trump’s fuel economy rollback, touting the move as the end to an EV mandate in the auto sector put in place by former President Joe Biden and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. Duffy also said that the move would make cars cheaper by $1,300 and result in savings worth $138 billion over five years.

Earlier, economist Peter Schiff had lamented the cost disparity between prices of vehicles in the U.S. and prices of “high-quality” Chinese vehicles in countries like Panama. Schiff pointed out that the vehicles were over half the cost of their U.S. counterparts.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Tuesday called the Republican-backed Ratepayer Protection Act "optional" and "toothless," arguing that it fails to impose binding safeguards as AI data centers drive higher electricity demand.

Schumer Calls Data Center Bill Optional, Toothless

"Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, but all Republicans offer is a toothless messaging bill," Schumer said on the Senate floor. "The bill is a fraud. I can sum up the shortcomings of Republicans’ data center bill with one word: optional." He later accused Republicans of seeking an "ineffectual participation trophy."

The House passed H.R. 9340 by 417-3 on Sept. 16 after lawmakers had moved to address household electricity costs tied to the data-center boom. The measure would establish a federal standard under which state regulators would consider requiring large-load customers with at least 100 megawatts of peak demand to cover the full incremental cost of generation, transmission and distribution upgrades needed to serve them.

However, the bill requires state regulators to consider that standard and make a determination within two years rather than compel states to adopt it.

Read Also: House Republicans Accuse China of ‘Throwing Gasoline on the Fire’ in US Data Center Fight — ‘They Want To Win The AI War’

Senate Fight Shifts To Data Center Costs

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) blocked Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) attempt to clear the legislation by unanimous consent and instead promoted his GRID Savings Act, which would direct federal regulators to require large-load customers to pay for facilities needed to connect them to the grid.

Husted calls his measure "the most meaningful bipartisan step Congress could take" to protect consumers from higher electricity prices. President Donald Trump has also discussed advancing the bill with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), as Republicans emphasize affordability ahead of November’s midterms.

AI Power Demand Raises Stakes For Ratepayers

The debate comes as AI infrastructure reshapes U.S. power demand. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates data centers could consume 11.8% of U.S. electricity by 2030, with scenarios ranging from 9.5% to 15.3%. The EIA, in a press release this month, said it expects electricity generation to rise 2.2% to a record level in 2026, citing data-center development as a major driver.

The White House has separately expanded its voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which technology companies and power providers commit to preventing data-center infrastructure costs from shifting to households.

"A guardrail that is optional isn’t a guardrail at all," Schumer said, urging Republicans to pursue "meaningful action" rather than what he described as "hollow proposals."

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) co-founder Steve Wozniak warned on Tuesday that artificial intelligence could replace humans by getting people so attached to chatbots that they stop having children, while analyst Gene Munster believes not enough people understand the power of these bots.

People Falling in Love With Chatbots

In a post on X, Wozniak said his “unique perspective” on how AI will replace humans will be that “so many fall in love with chatbots that they can’t have human children wish.”

A Northeastern University study earlier this month found that users are developing intense emotional attachments to AI chatbots, with researchers warning that the systems’ “sycophancy behavior” can reinforce harmful beliefs, even though they “cannot genuinely feel empathy.”

Personalized AI Bots Are About to ‘Blow Away’ Users

Meanwhile, Deepwater Asset Management‘s Gene Munster said personalized AI bots will “blow the everyday tech user away” over the next year, calling it good news for Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX), Apple, Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Cognition AI, Inc.

He added that his firm has been testing Siri, Grok, Meta’s Muse, Poke and Alphabet Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Gemini Spark, and has seen their usefulness “go off the charts” over the past month for everyday tasks like catching up on news and filtering spam.

Meta’s Muse, which launched Sept. 8, reached the top of the U.S. iOS free-app chart and topped 2.5 million downloads within two weeks, while Apple’s rebuilt Siri, shipped with iOS 27, still trails it on agentic capabilities, according to Bank of America’s Wamsi Mohan.

AI Safety Concerns Mount

OpenAI canceled its GPT-6.1 Astra release, citing internal safety standards, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, and Sam Altman have all pushed for stronger safeguards as AI agents grow more autonomous.

The debate on AI safety intensified after former Anthropic researcher put the odds of AI wiping out humanity within a decade above 10%.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), meanwhile, unveiled a new platform to prevent AI agents from breaching containment, partnering with Anthropic to integrate Claude’s cloud-managed agents into the system and enhance AI developer safety.

Kala Bio Inc. (NASDAQ:KALA) shares rose 57.10% to $0.79 in after-hours trading Tuesday after the company announced it had signed a non-binding letter of intent to acquire a nationwide telehealth platform.

KALA Bio is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company building an on-premises AI infrastructure platform for the biotechnology industry.

The Telehealth Target

KALA signed a non-binding letter of intent (LOI) on Sept. 24 to acquire 100% of a privately held management services organization supporting a telehealth platform serving clients in all 50 states, according to a press release. The target platform is LegitScript-certified and NABP-accredited.

The proposed acquisition is valued at approximately $15 million, payable in a combination of cash and KALA stock, with the cash portion funded from existing balance sheet resources.

The target generated approximately $12.7 million in revenue for the trailing twelve months ended August 2026, unaudited, and is cash-flow positive. Since its founding in 2023, the target has served more than 90,000 clients and generated over $48 million in sales, focused on GLP-1 weight management, hormone health, longevity and sexual wellness.

Minkowitz on the Deal

“This transaction would add an established, revenue-generating platform to KALA’s operating business,” said Avi Minkowitz, Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer of KALA. He said the company is targeting closing in late 2026 or early 2027, following a 45-day due diligence period expected to conclude in November 2026.

Congress has passed legislation to formally end production of the U.S. penny after more than 230 years, sending the bipartisan Common Cents Act to President Donald Trump after the Senate passed it by unanimous consent on Monday.

Congress Moves to Permanently Codify Penny Halt

The U.S. Mint had already stopped making circulating pennies in 2025 after Treasury concluded new one-cent coins were no longer needed.

The measure gives permanent legal backing to the production halt while keeping existing pennies legal tender. It also allows the Mint to continue limited collector issues and creates a national framework for businesses to round cash transactions to the nearest five cents when exact change is unavailable; electronic and other non-cash payments would still be charged to the exact cent.

Rising Production Costs Drive Penny’s Exit

The economics drove the change. The Mint says each penny now costs 3.69 cents to produce, up from 1.42 cents a decade ago, and ending circulating production should save about $56 million annually. Pennies accounted for 57% of the Mint’s 5.61 billion circulating coins in fiscal 2024, when it produced roughly 3.2 billion one-cent pieces.

"When it comes to taking on waste and making sure our tax dollars are spent wisely, it’s common sense that we should stop making a coin that costs nearly four times more than it’s worth to produce," Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), a co-sponsor with Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), said when the House advanced the legislation.

The legislation also authorizes Treasury to test a cheaper nickel composition if the alternative cuts production costs without materially disrupting vending machines and other coin-operated equipment.

Trump Order Preceded Congress’s Formal Action

Trump had already ordered Treasury in February 2025 to halt penny production, calling the coin wasteful and saying the U.S. had minted it "for far too long." The move subsequently raised questions about cash totals being rounded to the nearest nickel.

The Mint says consumers can continue spending pennies indefinitely. It also plans to keep producing limited numismatic versions, meaning the coin will disappear from routine production rather than vanish from wallets and collections overnight.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) pushed back against House Speaker Mike Johnson’s claim that opposition to data centers is linked to a Chinese psychological operation, arguing that Americans have legitimate concerns about the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

Sanders Challenges China Claim

On Tuesday, Sanders criticized Johnson in a post on X while sharing a clip from a Fox News interview in which Johnson discussed Democratic opposition to data centers.

"No, Mr. Johnson," Sanders wrote. "The 75% of Americans who oppose data centers, including a majority of Republicans, have not fallen victim to a Chinese psyop."

Sanders said Americans were "rightly concerned about AI billionaires raising their electricity bills, destroying the environment and threatening humanity."

Johnson Defends Data Center Stance

In the Fox News clip, the reporter asked Johnson about claims from technology executives and lawmakers that opposition to data centers was coming from China and about Democrats making the issue part of their midterm messaging.

"This is what Democrats do every election cycle," he said, accusing Democrats of focusing on "doom and gloom" messaging.

"Don’t buy it. It is a Chinese cy op," Johnson said. "I really believe that. And it’s not a conspiracy theory. I think they’re pushing those ideas."

AI Data Centers Faced Growing Scrutiny

Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) criticized the Republican-backed Ratepayer Protection Act as "optional" and "toothless," arguing it lacked binding safeguards for rising electricity demand from AI data centers. The House had passed the bill 417-3.

Previously, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) also warned that communities near data centers faced higher utility costs, strained water resources and environmental concerns, saying, "Americans shouldn’t be subsidizing the cost of these data centers."

China-Linked Data Center Probe

House Republicans Jason Smith (R-MO) and John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) asked Treasury and IRS officials to investigate whether China-linked funding supported U.S. groups opposing AI data centers.

They alleged that some organizations could be using tax-exempt status to advance foreign interests.

Smith and Moolenaar acknowledged legitimate concerns over electricity and water use but questioned whether China-linked groups were exploiting those concerns to slow U.S. AI development.

The lawmakers did not establish that all data center opposition was connected to China.

Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded over $3 billion in net inflows from Sept. 17 through Sept. 29, marking nine consecutive positive U.S. trading sessions.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (NASDAQ: IBIT), the world’s largest cryptocurrency-focused fund, alone pulled in more than $1 billion in inflows last week, according to data from SoSo Value.

The returns on long-dated 10-year Treasury notes climbed to 5.29% on Tuesday, its highest level since 2007, while the 30-year yield rose above 5.6%, reaching its highest level since June 2002.

Boeing Co. (NYSE:BA) has won a contract worth more than $20 billion to develop the U.S. Navy’s F/A-XX next-generation stealth fighter, beating Northrop Grumman Corp. (NYSE:NOC) and securing its second major sixth-generation fighter program in two years.

F/A-XX Brings Stealth, Range And Integration

The Pentagon said the full-scale development award covers multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems and weapons-integration testing. "F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter," Pentagon acquisition chief Michael Duffey said, calling the aircraft a "crucial, non-negotiable investment" in long-term U.S. air-combat capability.

The aircraft is intended to begin replacing the Navy’s F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers in the 2030s. Navy officials have previously said the sixth-generation platform should bring greater range, advanced sensors and lethality while integrating with crewed and uncrewed systems.

Read Also: NASA Chief Gives Boeing Starliner Second Chance After 2024 Mishap — Uncrewed Flight Could Come By Early 2027: ‘Fastest Path to Preserving Reliable Crewed Access’ to LEO

The award gives Boeing’s St. Louis defense operations a major next-generation fighter program as production of the Navy’s Super Hornets and Growlers winds down. Boeing Defense CEO Steve Parker said investments in "new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next-generation capabilities" leave the company ready to execute the program.

Boeing Secures Second Sixth-Generation Fighter Win

The victory follows Boeing’s 2025 win over Lockheed Martin for the Air Force’s F-47, another development contract worth more than $20 billion. That selection had already revived Boeing’s fighter business, while the F/A-XX award now places the company at the center of both services’ sixth-generation fighter efforts.

Delays Give Way To Long-Term Fleet Plan

The Navy competition had faced repeated delays over engineering and supply-chain capacity. The Pentagon considered pushing the program back by as much as three years before Congress intervened, providing $750 million in 2025 legislation and another $1.4 billion for fiscal 2026. Lockheed Martin was eliminated from the competition in March 2025, leaving Boeing and Northrop as finalists.

Reuters said the F/A-XX program could ultimately be worth hundreds of billions of dollars as production expands and potential foreign orders emerge. The Navy expects first production aircraft in the 2030s, with the F/A-XX operating alongside more than 270 planned F-35Cs while Super Hornets remain in service into the 2040s.

‘CNBC host Jim Cramer said Wall Street could be overreacting to the potential threat of Meta Platforms Inc.‘s (NASDAQ: META) Muse AI agent on consumer-focused industries. Cramer pointed to Airbnb Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) as one of the stocks “insulated” from AI competition.

Cramer Downplays Threat as Similar to SaaSpocalypse

The new AI-driven disruption called “consumer inertia” is a theory that AI agents like Muse will negatively impact companies that profit from consumer passivity — mainly when people neglect to cancel subscriptions, compare market pricing, or search for better deals.

On Tuesday, Cramer said on the Mad Money show that he was “skeptical” about selling off entire groups due to the belief that agentic AI will cause the "death of consumer inertia" and ruin the businesses that profit from it.

“I think Airbnb is mostly insulated from AI competition,” said Cramer, adding that it was easier for an agent to book a hotel online than to book directly from an owner of a property.

Cramer also talked about how Doordash Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH) was impacted by AI-displacement worries and its stock had tanked a few months ago, but since then it had rebounded.

Cramer said that he doesn’t think people would want to share their bank information with these agents, adding, “It doesn’t seem safe to me.” He draws a parallel to the previous enterprise software, which was known as SaaSpocalypse, noting that stocks did fall at the time but have since rebounded.

However, for investors, these remarks could be tough to digest because since Muse launched on Sept. 8, Planet Fitness Inc (NYSE:PLNT) has slumped about 20%, Booking Holdings Inc (NASDAQ:BKNG) has tumbled around 16%, while Airbnb has declined nearly 16%.

Muse a Revenue Driver for Meta and a Challenger to Apple?

A day ago, Cramer said that Meta must be viewed as an "enterprise company" after Muse AI was deployed. He noted that this operational shift could drive Meta’s stock valuation from an "18 times multiple" to "24-25."

Early adoption and potential subscription revenue have helped boost Meta’s stock. BNP Paribas analyst Nick Jones and analyst Gene Munster both highlighted different paths through which Muse could create additional value for the tech giant. Jones sees Meta’s existing apps helping drive additional downloads. Muse currently plans to monetize through small transaction fees, but BNP Paribas sees advertising as another potential longer-term opportunity.

Meanwhile, analysts at Bank of America Securities note that Muse has found Apple Inc.‘s (NASDAQ: AAPL) weak spot. By steering where users shop, book travel, or make payments, Muse risks stripping Apple of valuable discovery, referral, and transaction revenue — even as iPhone sales remain robust, according to the analysts.

Meta’s stock closed 3.24% higher at $738.79. In the past one month, the shares have surged 29.08%, while year-to-date the stock is up 11.92%. After hours, the stock climbed about 0.61% to $743.30.
